extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters learning how to write news stories about exhibitions, entertainments, special occasions, and group interviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing news stories about exhibitions, shows, fairs, parades, banquets, holiday celebrations, and groups of interviews — focusing on purpose, selection of detail, treatment, and formats for presenting multiple interviews or speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story (two classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in this division may be grouped in two classes: (1) those of display, such as exhibitions, shows, fairs, and parades, and (2) those of banquets, holiday celebrations, and other special occasions, such as college commencements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the subject matter covers a wide range, the method of handling the news is much the same for both classes; classify the event to decide emphasis (display vs. social/ceremonial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — portray events and bring out spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim in these stories is not only to portray attractively the events and scenes but to bring out the spirit of the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and present details from the point of view of their value as showing the mood of the occasion — this yields a more interesting story than merely recording incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy as truth of sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy in news stories of this kind, therefore, is not simply faithfulness to fact, but truth of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding fictitious details to heighten appeal and avoid substituting sentimentality for true sentiment; fidelity includes correct portrayal of the occasion's mood and tone as well as facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — select picturesque and significant phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief problem in writing these stories is to select picturesque and significant phases from the large mass of available material, and to reproduce the scenes and incidents with vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These events offer one of the few chances in news writing for pure description. Choose details that will vividly reproduce the scene and support the dominant impression you wish to convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic description — bring out one impression
rubrics_metrics.description: In general the description is of the so-called dynamic type, in that all of the details are selected with the purpose of bringing out one impression rather than of giving a complete picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor focused, impression-driven descriptions over encyclopedic completeness; shape details to reinforce the single dominant note of the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of emotional appeal matched to holiday/occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: In descriptions of holiday celebrations an emotional appeal is possible because every festival and holiday has its own particular sentiment (e.g., Christmas — generosity; Memorial Day — patriotic reverence; Fourth of July — patriotic jollification; Thanksgiving — feasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For banquets and occasions where good fellowship is dominant, use a lighter descriptive vein; select details that amplify the occasion's characteristic emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling speeches and toasts
rubrics_metrics.description: When speeches and toasts are delivered in connection with these events, they are treated like other speeches and are fitted into the story as incidents of the occasion, or, if they are of sufficient significance, they may be played up as the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a speech is an incidental detail (embed briefly) or the feature (quote/expand) based on its significance to the occasion's dominant note or news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group interviews — formats and representative quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting a group of interviews on the same subject, there are different formats for presenting several interviews: (a) a sequence of short attributed reactions from various people, (b) telegraph/wire style with context and representative official statements, (c) mixed formats combining brief quotes and factual context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the leading context (e.g., decision or event), then present representative voices with clear attribution; adapt the format to space, medium (telegraph/wire), and the need to show the range of reaction (use short pithy quotes or slightly expanded statements as appropriate).
